title: Set Matrix Zeroes: first row/column as markers.
shortTitle: Set Matrix Zeroes: using the first row and column as in-place markers
keyPoints: If any cell is zero, its entire row and entire column must be set to zero, done in place with O(1) extra space.
The first row and first column are reused as marker storage to record which rows and columns must be zeroed.
Two boolean flags are saved first to remember whether the first row and first column themselves originally contained a zero.
The algorithm has four phases: save flags, mark, zero inner cells, then zero first row and column last.
Order matters: inner cells must be zeroed before the first row and column, or the markers are destroyed.
Time complexity is O(m * n); the entire matrix is traversed a constant number of times.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use the first row and first column as your zero-marker notepad so you need only constant extra memory.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Set Matrix Zeroes** – if any cell in an m-by-n matrix is zero, its entire row and entire column must be set to zero.
- **In-place markers** – the first row and first column are reused as marker storage, recording which rows and columns need zeroing.
- **Saved flags** – two boolean flags record whether the first row and first column originally contained a zero, since they are about to be overwritten with markers.
- **Four phases** – (1) save flags, (2) mark using first row/column, (3) zero inner cells, (4) zero first row/column.
- **Complexity** – O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a reconciliation grid has rows for dates and columns for branches. A zero means a frozen entry. Policy requires the entire date (row) and entire branch (column) to be wiped. Instead of a separate notepad, Priya writes the flags in the margin of the grid itself, the top row and left column, then wipes in one careful pass.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Original Matrix:
  ┌───┬───┬───┐
  │ 1 │ 1 │ 1 │
  ├───┼───┼───┤
  │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │  ← zero at [1][1]
  ├───┼───┼───┤
  │ 1 │ 1 │ 1 │
  └───┴───┴───┘

Phase 1: Save flags
  firstRowZero = false, firstColZero = false

Phase 2: Mark (write into first row/col)
  matrix[1][0] = 0  (row 1 marker)
  matrix[0][1] = 0  (col 1 marker)
  ┌───┬───┬───┐
  │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │  ← col marker
  ├───┼───┼───┤
  │ 0 │ 0 │ 1 │  ← row marker
  ├───┼───┼───┤
  │ 1 │ 1 │ 1 │
  └───┴───┴───┘

Phase 3: Zero inner cells using markers
  ┌───┬───┬───┐
  │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │
  ├───┼───┼───┤
  │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │  ← row 1 zeroed
  ├───┼───┼───┤
  │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │  ← col 1 zeroed
  └───┴───┴───┘

Phase 4: First row/col (flags were false, skip)
  Final result: same as above
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Set Matrix Zeroes requires that if any cell is zero, its entire row and column are zeroed, and the in-place challenge is doing this with only constant extra space. The elegant technique reuses the first row and first column as marker storage, recording which rows and columns need zeroing without allocating separate sets.

The algorithm has four phases. First, I save two boolean flags for whether the first row and first column originally contain a zero. Second, I scan the inner matrix and mark zeros into the first row and column. Third, I zero inner cells based on those markers. Fourth, I use the saved flags to decide whether to zero the first row and column themselves.

The order is critical. If I zeroed the first row or column before using the markers, I would destroy the information I need for the inner cells. The two-flag approach is clearer and less error-prone than the single-flag variant. The entire algorithm runs in O(m * n) time with O(1) extra space.

At the National Bank of India, a reconciliation grid had rows for dates and columns for branches, and a zero meant a discrepancy requiring quarantine across the whole date and branch. The in-place marker technique kept the nightly reconciliation job within its memory budget.

Remember one sentence: save two flags, mark into the first row and column, zero the inner cells, then zero the borders last.
